extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of drama/poetics (playwrights, critics, literary scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing and evaluating tragic drama according to Aristotelian Poetics as interpreted in a literary textbook: what emotions, plot-structure, character-types, and artistic conditions produce a full tragic effect (katharsis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity and fear combined
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy must evoke both pity (ἔλεος) and fear (φόβος); the 'requirement of Aristotle is pity and fear.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The full tragic effect requires the union of the two emotions; an inferior tragedy may excite only one. The text argues against views that pity alone or fear alone suffice, noting passages where Aristotle treats them jointly (Poet. xi, xiv). Modern drama often emphasizes pity over fear (e.g., most moderns except Shakespeare), and eighteenth-century French tragedy largely eliminated fear. Avoid producing works that evoke only sentimental pity or mere terror without the allied emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity targets the undeserving (ὁ ἀνάξιος)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pity has for its object 'the misfortunes of one who is undeserving' (ὁ ἀνάξιος)—i.e., a person who meets with sufferings beyond his deserts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's notion does not demand an absolutely innocent sufferer but someone suffering undeservedly; at moments pity will predominate where the action highlights the undeserved nature of suffering. Compare Rhetoric distinctions between disinterested and self-regarding pity. Use characters whose misfortunes appear excessive relative to their deserts to elicit pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear arises from moral resemblance (ὁ ὅμοιος)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear in tragedy is 'περὶ τὸν ὅμοιον'—felt for a character morally like ourselves; tragic φόβος is a sympathetic shudder inspired by resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragic fear is not the direct apprehension of personal danger but an imaginative identification with a hero whose essential character resembles our own. Emphasize qualities in the protagonist that allow the audience to see themselves in him/her so that impending misfortune produces fear for ourselves in imaginative sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic fear as imaginative identification (not literal self-fear)
rubrics_metrics.description: The φόβος of tragedy differs from real-life fear; it is an imaginative shudder and tension produced by sympathetic identification, not immediate fear for one's own life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fear 'is the sympathetic shudder we feel for a hero'—a thrill, foreboding, or awe rather than a crushing personal terror. Craft scenes that generate agonised expectation and imaginative involvement (e.g., Oedipus Tyrannus). Avoid equating tragic fear with mere anticipation of a future event in a literal, self-regarding sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero must be elevated yet fallible
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic hero should be morally like us but elevated in dignity—'not a man of flawless perfection, nor of consummate villainy'—possessing a rich humanity with frailties and imperfections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should rise above common level in dignity and moral elevation while retaining human flaws so that we can identify with them yet feel the grandeur and distance necessary for tragic effect. Avoid purely biographical or wholly exemplary characters (perfect saints or monsters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter must be universal and significant
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic action must admit of being universalised; the deeds and fortunes shown should attach to larger issues so the spectator is lifted above the particular case to universal law or human destiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy requires that suffering be exhibited in a comprehensive aspect and connected to public or elemental concerns (example: Romeo and Juliet's family feud makes the lovers' fate of public consequence). Parochial, bourgeois, or narrowly private subjects (the ordinary domestic struggles typical of some Ibsen plays) tend to retain a sense of triviality and cannot easily produce the solemnity and awe of genuine tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Katharsis: purification/expulsion of painful elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic katharsis involves the expulsion of the disturbing painful element in pity and fear and the purifying of those emotions so that pain gives way to a pleasurable, refined satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotelian katharsis is seen as a refining process: art removes selfish or egoistic taints from pity and fear, converting mixed/painful feelings into noble pleasure. This is an aesthetic, not a direct moral, operation—tragedy acts on feelings rather than on the will. The textbook emphasises that the painful element is expelled when the emotion is universalised and deprived of self-centredness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (organic, causal whole)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy must exhibit unity of action: a single, complete, and 'whole' action in which successive incidents are linked by necessary and probable causal sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity is an inward organic principle: parts must be arranged in fixed order and structurally related so that none can be removed or transposed without harming the organism. Unity of action (not unity of the hero or person) is the first requirement. Emphasise causal necessity/probability rather than accident or loose episodic aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate magnitude (μέγεθος) and eurymnemonic scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The action must have a magnitude sufficient for natural development but limited enough that the mind can grasp and retain it (e.g., not so vast as the Trojan War).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a scale that allows the decisive change of fortune to evolve freely and fully; the whole should be 'easily remembered' (εὐμνημόνευτον) and amenable to apprehension. Avoid extremes that make the plot ungraspable or trivial in scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginning, middle, and end (structural completeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole must have a beginning (not itself the necessary consequence of something else), a middle (causally connected between beginning and end), and an end (follows from something but has nothing following it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a natural, definite starting point and ending point for the action so antecedents do not force endless retrogression. The middle is defined by causal connectivity (not mere temporal sequence). Ensure the poet selects points that make the action complete in itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denouement must arise from the plot (no deus ex machina)
rubrics_metrics.description: The λύσις (unravelling/denouement) must arise out of the plot itself, not by recourse to accident or deus ex machina.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid contrived fifth-act rescues or arbitrary resolutions that do not follow from prior causal structure. The text warns that many bad plays perish in an indifferent fifth act—'of what? of the fifth act'—and Lessing's anecdote is cited as anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (ἀναγνώρισις) and reversal (περιπέτεια) woven into plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal of the situation (περιπέτεια) and recognition (ἀναγνώρισις) are powerful devices that intensify tragic emotion but must be discovered as inevitable consequences of prior events, woven into the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex (πεπλεγμένη) plots that use recognition and reversal are preferred by Aristotle for heightening emotion, but these surprises must be organic—not arbitrary—and should be revealed as necessary though unexpected results of what has gone before.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidents must be necessary and probable (causal plausibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Successive incidents should be connected by inward and causal bonds—necessary or probable sequence—so each event follows as a natural consequence of preceding events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise internal necessity and plausibility in plotting. Avoid coincidences, gratuitous episodes, or episodes that break the causal chain; even reversals and recognitions must appear inevitable in hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic representation amplifies and modifies emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Under conditions of scenic representation (speech, gesture, costume) pity and fear are often intensified or modified compared with their forms in real life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use staging, acting, and sensory elements to heighten pathos and produce more moving effects than narrative alone. Aristotle notes that theatrical means can make actions appear nearer and more pitiable than mere report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exclusive self-absorbed motives (e.g., private love alone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotions that are exclusive and self-centred (like narrow private love) resist kathartic treatment; tragic motives should rest on permanent and objective realities rather than individual caprice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While romantic passion can be tragic, it attains true tragedy only when set against larger social or public issues (example: Romeo and Juliet's family feud). Avoid relying on purely private, egoistic motives that cannot be generalised into universal significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action must allow decisive change of fortune via causal sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: The play should be of sufficient size and structure to permit a decisive change of fortune (from good to bad or vice versa) to occur through the causal unfolding of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a condition for both simple (ἁπλῆ πρᾶξις) and complex (πεπλεγμένη) plots. Ensure the plot's magnitude and causal connectivity permit a believable and significant reversal of fortune central to tragic design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic pleasure: transport through universalised emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinctive tragic pleasure resides in the transport of feeling that lifts the spectator beyond the individual self into an enlarged sympathy—a 'noble emotional satisfaction' produced by purified pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for an emotional resolution in which selfish elements drop away and the spectator experiences awe, calm, and refined enjoyment. This is the aesthetic end of tragedy rather than direct moral instruction; design the work to produce this elevation.
